[163] 6. Intellectual property is NOT defined as (highlight or underline your answer)
[164] cultural knowledge or artifacts that can be turned into profit.
[165] gaining wealth from traditional knowledge, and sharing it equally amongst all responsible for its creation.
[166] having exclusive rights to a variety of intangible assets, such as musical, literary, and artistic works.
[167] artifacts appropriated and made the property of non-indigenous people or corporations.

[353] Assignment 4.3 Contemporary Issues /20 Marks
[354] How do you think the Indigenous population situation in Canada compares to the information that you have discovered about Australia? Research and summarize the current situation regarding oil pipelines between Alberta and B.C.  What are the different  Aboriginal viewpoints? What are the viewpoints of the government? Include provincial and federal. Discuss how the political climate changed recently. Include any attempts to heal and move forward. What are some arguments that various groups are using? Using the evidence provided above as your starting point, and at least two recent news articles dated at least January 2017, answer the questions in a multi paragraph detailed response. Be sure to include at least one quote and provide a link to your articles.

[393] 13. What does the Rio Declaration of 1992 state? Why is this declaration important for indigenous people? -457199476252
[397] 14. For each industry, match the specific explanation of how the activities of this industry can have positive and/or negative effects on indigenous populations.   Industries:  Tourism, Petroleum, Forestry, Mining, Hydroelectricity.  You can use the terms more than once.-5714991238257
[399] Forestry - Can lead to partnerships supporting animal sanctuaries across the world.
[401] Mining - Extraction of raw materials has led to environmental damage, pollution, and has displaced populations
[403] Tourism - Can lend to encroaching land and rights of indigenous peoples.
[405] Hydroelectricity - Usually involves creating dams, which has flooded traditional areas of indigenous peoples, causing many groups to be relocated
[407] Mining - This industry is Canada’s largest employer of Aboriginal people.
[409] Forestry - This industry has taken traditional lands and plants from groups that use native plants for medicinal purposes.
[411] Petroleum -  High demand for oil has left significant environmental damage and a long list of offenses against indigenous populations

[570] Use the ‘Fact Sheet’ below to answer the following questions.
[571] Fact Sheet
[572] Canada's Aboriginal population is growing 3.5 times faster than the general population.
[573] By 2026, the Aboriginal population is projected to make up 4.6 percent of the Canadian population (1 in 25 people).
[574] The Aboriginal population is much younger than the overall Canadian population
[575] In the next 20 years an estimated 30% of Canadians will be retired.
[576] Young adults without a high school diploma or employment are more at risk of committing crimes that lead to being incarcerated.
[577] Suicide rates are five to seven times higher for First Nations youth than for non-Aboriginal youth.
[578] The unemployment rate among Aboriginal people is 14%, compared to 6% among non-Aboriginal people.
[579] The rate of First Nation graduation is 36% compared to the Canadian graduation rate of 72%.
[580] 61% of First Nation young adults aged 20-24 have not completed high school, compared with 13% of non-Aboriginal people in Canada.
[581] Less than 4% of the population in Canada is aboriginal, yet they represent 17% of all provincial inmates in custody and 13% of all federal prisoners.
[582] The annual average cost of keeping a Canadian inmate incarcerated is $113,974 per year.
[583] The annual average cost of educating a student in Canada is $6,667 per year.
